points.description: Shows that for sufficiently large n, n^k has exactly k digits in base 2n (i.e. (2n)^{k-1} ≤ n^k < (2n)^k, using n ≥ 2^{k-1}), so the digits are indexed i = 0,…,k-1.

levels.says: States that n^k has k digits but justification is incomplete or only one of the two inequalities is shown.

points.description: Expresses the digits correctly, e.g. the i-th digit a_i = ⌊n^k/(2n)^i⌋ mod 2n (or equivalent expansion n^k = Σ a_i (2n)^i with 0 ≤ a_i < 2n).

Computes or determines the digits explicitly using n odd, e.g. n^k = (2n)^{k-1}·n/2^{k-1} and expanding in powers of 2n, so that each digit is given by a closed form/polynomial-type expression (depending on parity of n) of size about n/2^{k-1-i}, or equivalently shows each digit grows with n.

levels.says: Begins the explicit computation with the right idea (using oddness of n) but computation is incorrect or incomplete.

points.description: Shows each digit (including the lowest and highest) exceeds d for n larger than a chosen explicit N depending on k and d, and concludes the proof.

levels.says: Handles most digits but misses a case (e.g. the last digit) or does not clearly choose N.

rubric.notes: Full marks need a complete proof: k digits, digit formula, explicit digit evaluation using n odd, and the bound exceeding d for large n. Partial credit for showing the digit count and digit expression only. Equivalent wording and correct alternative methods earn the marks.
